comparisons.peer_topic: 2024 Provision for Credit Losses drivers and amount
comparisons.peer_summary: The provision for credit losses increased $1.4 billion to $5.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023, primarily driven by credit card and small business loan growth, as well as asset quality deterioration in commercial real estate office and credit card portfolios.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Bank of America reported increases in their provision for credit losses driven primarily by credit card portfolio performance. Goldman Sachs' provision rose to $1.54 billion from $1.14 billion, with net provisions reflected by the credit card portfolio driven by net charge-offs. Similarly, Bank of America's provision increased by $1.4 billion to $5.8 billion, also primarily driven by credit card loan growth. However, Bank of America additionally cited asset quality deterioration in the commercial real estate office portfolio and small business loan growth as key drivers, whereas Goldman Sachs' disclosure focuses exclusively on the credit card portfolio and net charge-offs for this segment.

sentences.text: Provision for credit losses was $1.54 billion for 2024, compared with $1.14 billion for 2023.
Provisions for 2024 reflected net provisions related to the credit card portfolio (primarily driven by net charge-offs).
The provision for credit losses increased $1.4 billion to $5.8 billion for 2024 compared to 2023.

The provision for credit losses for 2024 was primarily driven by credit card as well as small business loan growth, and asset quality deterioration in the commercial real estate office and credit card portfolios.

comparisons.peer_summary: Net credit losses increased 40% to $9.0 billion, with consumer net credit losses rising 39% to $8.6 billion and corporate net credit losses increasing to $397 million from $250 million.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures identify credit card portfolios as a primary driver of increased credit losses. Goldman Sachs reported a provision increase driven by net charge-offs in its credit card portfolio. Citigroup reported a 40% increase in net credit losses to $9.0 billion, with consumer net credit losses (largely Branded Cards) rising 39%. While both highlight credit card deterioration, Citigroup quantifies the absolute dollar increase in net credit losses ($9.0 billion total), whereas Goldman Sachs quantifies the provision expense ($1.54 billion) and attributes it specifically to credit card net charge-offs.

sentences.text: Provisions for 2024 reflected net provisions related to the credit card portfolio (primarily driven by net charge-offs).
Consumer net credit losses of $8.6 billion increased 39%, largely reflecting the continued rise in net credit loss rates in Branded Cards and Retail Services.

comparisons.peer_topic: Provision for Credit Losses and Allowance Metrics
comparisons.peer_summary: The provision for credit losses was $10.7 billion (up from $9.3 billion prior year), reflecting $8.6 billion in net charge-offs driven by Card Services and a $2.0 billion net addition to the allowance, which totaled $26.9 billion at year-end.
comparisons.comparison: Both companies reported an increase in their provision for credit losses driven significantly by Card Services portfolios. Goldman Sachs' provision increased to $1.54 billion, driven by net provisions in the credit card portfolio. JPMorgan's provision increased to $10.7 billion from $9.3 billion, with net charge-offs driven by Card Services reflecting the seasoning of vintages and credit normalization. While both cite credit card activity as a driver, JPMorgan provides a detailed breakdown of the allowance build ($2.0 billion net addition) and higher absolute charge-offs ($8.6 billion), whereas Goldman Sachs links the provision rise directly to credit card net charge-offs without detailing the allowance movement in this specific sentence.

sentences.text: Provision for credit losses was $1.54 billion for 2024, compared with $1.14 billion for 2023.
Provisions for 2024 reflected net provisions related to the credit card portfolio (primarily driven by net charge-offs).

• The provision for credit losses was $10.7 billion, reflecting $8.6 billion of net charge-offs and a net addition to the allowance for credit losses of $2.0 billion. Net charge-offs increased by $2.4 billion, driven by Card Services, reflecting the seasoning of vintages originated in recent years, credit normalization, and balance growth. The net addition to the allowance for credit losses included a net addition of $2.1 billion in consumer, driven by Card Services, and a net reduction of $19 million in wholesale.
